desc:
A knight stands on cell (startRow, startCol) of an m x n board (0-indexed). A knight move changes the position by (+-2, +-1) or (+-1, +-2) and must stay on the board. A tour is a sequence of moves that visits every cell exactly once, starting on the given cell.

Write each visited cell as the pair (row, col) and compare two tours by their sequences of cells, from the first cell on: at the first position where they differ, the tour with the smaller pair (smaller row first, then smaller column) is the smaller tour. Return the board of the smallest tour, where result[r][c] is the step at which cell (r, c) is visited (1 for the starting cell, up to m * n). If no tour exists, return an empty array [].

For example, for m = 3, n = 4 and start (0, 0) the answer is [[1,4,7,10],[8,11,2,5],[3,6,9,12]]: from the corner the knight can go to (1,2) or (2,1), and (1,2) is smaller.
hints: Build the tour one cell at a time, as a DFS over knight moves that never revisits a cell, and undo a move when the rest of the tour cannot be completed.

Trying the next cells in increasing (row, col) order guarantees that the first complete tour you find is the smallest one in the required comparison. Return as soon as the tour is complete; do not look at other tours.

Without pruning the search can be slow on 5 x 5. Keep for every cell the number of unvisited cells a knight could still reach from it. After you move, a neighbour of the new cell whose count dropped to 0 can only be the final cell of the tour: if more than one cell remains, abandon the branch.
editorial: The comparison in the statement is exactly the order in which a depth-first search tries its candidates when the eight knight offsets are listed so that the destination cells come out in increasing (row, col) order. That order is (-2,-1), (-2,+1), (-1,-2), (-1,+2), (+1,-2), (+1,+2), (+2,-1), (+2,+1). The first time the DFS manages to place all m * n cells, the tour found is the smallest one, because every smaller prefix was tried and failed first.

Plain backtracking explores a huge number of dead ends on boards like 5 x 5. A sound pruning rule keeps the answer unchanged: store the number of unvisited neighbours for each cell. When the knight moves, those counts drop for the neighbours of the new cell. An unvisited cell with no unvisited neighbour left can still be entered right now but can never be left, so it must be the very last cell. If more than one cell remains, no tour exists below this branch. With this rule every board of at most 25 cells is solved well within the time limit. Warnsdorff's heuristic (always go to the neighbour with fewest exits) is faster, but it does not produce the smallest tour, so it cannot be used here.
time: exponential in the worst case; fast with pruning
